html:
A pandemic that struck the Roman Empire from about 249 to 262, perhaps lasting to 270, in the worst years of the Crisis of the Third Century. It takes its name from Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who described it in his sermon On the Mortality.

Victims had fever, diarrhoea, bleeding eyes and lost limbs or hearing. The cause is unknown; smallpox, measles and a fever like Ebola have all been suggested. One later source says that at its height 5,000 people a day died in Rome. It killed the young emperor Hostilian in 251.

It came on top of war and money troubles and left the army and farms short of men. Christian writers stressed that believers cared for the sick of all faiths, and some historians think this helped Christianity grow. It followed the Antonine Plague and came before the Plague of Justinian.
